title: Christianity: love is patient
hookLine: Paul's hymn to love: patient, kind, not envious (1 Corinthians 13, where the KJV says "charity")

lines: A COUSIN READS AT A WEDDING.
cards: If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard it. Someone's cousin walks to the front, unfolds a piece of paper, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone nods.
It's lovely. It fits on a card. But the man who wrote it wasn't thinking about weddings at all.

He was writing to a church that was falling apart: people suing each other, showing off, forming cliques, looking down on the ones with less. Today: Paul's chapter on love, and the fight it was written into.

teach.b: The writer is Paul, and the church is in Corinth, a busy Greek port city.
His first letter to them is full of their problems: rival factions, lawsuits, rich members eating well at the shared meal while poorer ones went hungry.
And the Corinthians were proud of their spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, knowledge.

teach.h: WITHOUT LOVE, ALL OF IT IS NOISE.
teach.b: So in chapter thirteen Paul says, in effect: without love, all of that is noise.
Then he describes love, and the King James Version says it like this: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Why charity?
The Greek word is agape, from the same family of words the Gospels use in the two commandments from a few days ago.

Latin translators rendered it caritas, and the King James translators followed with charity, which in their English meant a deep, self-giving love, not only giving money. Newer translations tend to say love.
Suffereth long is today's line: love is patient. Read it knowing it was written to people who were quarreling, and it isn't a description of a feeling.

teach.h: NOT A FEELING: A LIST OF BEHAVIORS.
teach.b: It's a list of behaviors, almost a job description.
Not showing off. Not easily provoked. Paul ends the chapter: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."

Christians read this chapter at weddings and funerals, and some also read it as a picture of how God loves. For a church that was falling apart, the instructions were simple: be patient with each other first.

how: 1 Corinthians 13 is read at many Christian weddings and funerals, and some Christians use its list, patient, kind, not envious, as a daily check on how they treat others.

o: giving money to the poor, as charity means now
self-giving love, shown in patience and kindness
romantic love, the kind read aloud at weddings

p: a Greek port city with a divided church
the Greek word for this love
the King James word, from caritas

s: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians 13 for a wedding
he wrote it to a quarreling church in Corinth.
in the King James Version, charity means a deep, self-giving love
from the Latin caritas, which rendered Greek agape.
Paul says without love, even great spiritual gifts are empty noise
he tells the proud Corinthians their gifts mean nothing without it.

games.q: your church is split into factions and everyone is proud of their gifts. what does Paul write?
o: a hymn to love: patient, kind, not puffed up.
games.why: he writes 1 Corinthians 13: without love, the rest is noise, and love is patient first.

practice: Bring to mind the person who tries your patience most, the slow one, the loud one, the one who never replies, and picture the moment it usually snaps.
Now replay that moment slowed down, with one breath before you answer: suffereth long. Rehearse that breath a few times.

wordCard.voice: Christianity, through Paul's hymn: agape, love that is patient and kind, written to a church in pieces. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love, the self-giving kind; Latin caritas, KJV charity.

carryVoice: Your line: love is patient. It comes first on Paul's list. That's day two hundred fifty-eight.
